title: Fried Egg
subtitle: Crisp lacy edges, a runny yolk, fried in butter
excerpt: A perfectly fried egg has crisp, golden-edged whites and a yolk that runs the moment you break it. Butter gives you the colour and flavour that oil never quite manages.
sourceNotes: The butter-fried egg is the standard British breakfast technique. Basting the yolk with hot butter is the classic method for cooking the surface without flipping.

glossaryTerms.definition: To spoon hot fat repeatedly over food as it cooks, here, tipping the pan and spooning hot butter over the egg yolk to set the surface without flipping.

content.text: A fried egg is one of the fastest things you can cook and one of the easiest to get wrong. The goal is a white that is fully set and lightly crisp at the edges, with a yolk that is warm but still liquid at the centre. Butter is the fat that gets you there, it browns lightly in the heat and coats the white with flavour that a neutral oil simply cannot match. The technique that makes it reliable is
: tilting the pan and spooning the hot butter back over the yolk so it cooks from above without any flipping.

Use a small frying pan. A 20 cm pan is the right size for one or two eggs. A pan that is too large spreads the butter thin before the egg arrives, and you lose the pooled fat you need for basting. Place the pan over a medium heat and add {{unsalted-butter}} butter. Let it melt and begin to foam. The moment the foam starts to subside and the butter smells faintly nutty, the pan is ready. Crack each {{eggs}} egg into a cup first, then slide it gently into the pan, this lets you check for shell and gives you control over where the yolk lands.

Once the egg is in the pan, tilt it slightly towards you so the butter pools at the edge. Use a spoon to scoop up the hot butter and pour it slowly over the yolk. Repeat every twenty seconds or so for two to three minutes. The white sets from the bottom up while the basted butter cooks the yolk surface just enough to turn it from raw and shiny to a pale, opaque film. The yolk underneath stays liquid. Finish with a pinch of {{sea-salt-flakes}} sea salt flakes scattered directly over the top.

Olive oil gives you a crispier, more frilled edge and a slightly lighter result. Butter gives you a softer edge with more flavour and a little browning on the underside of the white. Both are good choices, the decision is mostly about what you are eating alongside. For toast and a full breakfast plate, butter is the classic call. For eggs served with something bold and spiced, a neutral oil keeps the egg from competing.

The basting method is the British and French approach, the egg never flips, and the yolk is cooked by the basted fat alone. This is sometimes called sunny side up. Over-easy is an American technique where the egg is flipped briefly to set the yolk surface from direct heat. If you prefer a yolk with no runny film on top but still soft inside, a quick flip for fifteen seconds achieves that without the risk of overcooking. Either way, the egg comes out of the pan the moment the white is fully opaque and no longer jiggles, the yolk will carry on cooking from residual heat if you leave it in the pan too long.

Slide the egg onto hot buttered toast or a warm plate, a cold plate sets the white before you get to eat it. A fried egg belongs on a full cooked breakfast, tucked next to back bacon and grilled tomato, or on its own with thick brown bread and a scrape of salted butter. It is also one of the best things you can put on top of leftover bubble and squeak, which fries up in the same pan after the egg comes out.
White is set but yolk is hard: the heat was too high, or you basted too aggressively with very hot fat. Use medium rather than medium-high, and keep the basting gentle and slow.

White is still clear around the yolk when the edges are already brown: the pan was too hot. The white sets unevenly when the temperature spikes. Lower the heat and add a splash of water to the pan, then cover briefly, the steam finishes the white without overcooking the edges.

Butter is burning before the egg is ready: the pan was too hot when the butter went in. Start with the pan on medium and wait until the butter foams rather than immediately browns before cracking the egg.
